title: Breathing and Exchange of Gases
syllabus: Respiratory organs in animals (recall only); Respiratory system in humans; Mechanism of breathing and its regulation in humans - Exchange of gases, transport of gases and regulation of respiration; Respiratory volumes and capacities; Disorders related to respiration - Asthma, Emphysema, Occupational respiratory disorders.

questions.question: Which of the following respiratory volumes cannot be measured directly using a standard clinical spirometer?
questions.solution: Residual Volume (RV) is the volume of air remaining in the lungs even after a forceful expiration. Because it never leaves the lungs during breathing maneuvers, it cannot be measured directly by spirometry (along with capacities containing it, like FRC and TLC).

questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the respiratory organs across various animal groups:

List-I (Animal Group)List-II (Respiratory Organ)
(A) Earthworms(I) Moist cuticle (cutaneous respiration)
(B) Insects(II) Tracheal tubes (spiracles and tracheae)
(C) Aquatic arthropods and Molluscs(III) Gills (branchial respiration)
(D) Birds and Mammals(IV) Vascularised lungs (pulmonary respiration)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution: Earthworms respire through their moist cuticle; Insects use a network of tracheal tubes; Aquatic arthropods (prawns) and molluscs use gills; Terrestrial vertebrates (reptiles, birds, mammals) use vascularised lungs.

questions.question: During quiet, resting inspiration in humans, the primary muscular contractions that expand the thoracic cavity are:
options: Contraction of the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles
Contraction of internal intercostal muscles and abdominal muscles
Relaxation of the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles
questions.solution: Normal inspiration is initiated by the contraction of the diaphragm (which moves downward, increasing thoracic volume in the antero-posterior axis) and the contraction of external intercostal muscles (which lifts the ribs and sternum, increasing volume in the dorso-ventral axis).

questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II regarding respiratory volumes/capacities and their average physiological values in healthy adult humans:

List-I (Volume / Capacity)List-II (Standard Value)
(A) Tidal Volume (TV)(I) $2500 - 3000\text{ mL}$
(B) Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV)(II) $1000 - 1100\text{ mL}$
(C) Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV)(III) $1100 - 1200\text{ mL}$
(D) Residual Volume (RV)(IV) $500\text{ mL}$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution: Tidal Volume (TV) = $500\text{ mL}$; Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV) = $2500 - 3000\text{ mL}$; Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV) = $1000 - 1100\text{ mL}$; Residual Volume (RV) = $1100 - 1200\text{ mL}$.

questions.question: Vital Capacity (VC) of the human lung is mathematically represented by which of the following combinations?
questions.solution: Vital Capacity (VC) is the maximum volume of air a person can breathe in after a forced expiration (or breathe out after a forced inspiration): $$\text{VC} = \text{ERV} + \text{TV} + \text{IRV} \approx 3500 - 4500\text{ mL}$$

questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the partial pressures of oxygen ($p\text{O}_2$) and carbon dioxide ($p\text{CO}_2$) in different respiratory sites:

List-I (Site / Fluid)List-II ($p\text{O}_2$ and $p\text{CO}_2$ in $\text{mm Hg}$)
(A) Alveoli(I) $p\text{O}_2 = 40,\; p\text{CO}_2 = 45$
(B) Deoxygenated blood(II) $p\text{O}_2 = 95,\; p\text{CO}_2 = 40$
(C) Oxygenated blood(III) $p\text{O}_2 = 104,\; p\text{CO}_2 = 40$
(D) Tissues(IV) $p\text{O}_2 = 40,\; p\text{CO}_2 = 45$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution: In alveoli: $p\text{O}_2 = 104\text{ mm Hg}, p\text{CO}_2 = 40\text{ mm Hg}$; Deoxygenated blood: $p\text{O}_2 = 40\text{ mm Hg}, p\text{CO}_2 = 45\text{ mm Hg}$; Oxygenated blood: $p\text{O}_2 = 95\text{ mm Hg}, p\text{CO}_2 = 40\text{ mm Hg}$; Tissues: $p\text{O}_2 = 40\text{ mm Hg}, p\text{CO}_2 = 45\text{ mm Hg}$.

questions.question: The diffusion membrane across which alveolar gas exchange takes place consists of three essential layers with a total thickness of less than a millimeter. These three layers are:
options: Thin squamous epithelium of alveoli, endothelium of alveolar capillaries, and the basement substance between them
Ciliated columnar epithelium of bronchioles, smooth muscle layer, and pleural membrane
Non-keratinized stratified epithelium, tunica media, and fibrous connective tissue
Cuboidal alveolar epithelium, surfactant lining, and erythrocyte membrane
questions.solution: The diffusion membrane consists of 3 microscopic layers: (1) thin squamous epithelium of alveoli, (2) endothelium of alveolar capillaries, and (3) basement substance in between them. Its total thickness is much less than a millimetre ($0.2\text{ mm}$), facilitating rapid gas diffusion.

questions.question: The solubility of carbon dioxide ($\text{CO}_2$) in blood is how many times higher than that of oxygen ($\text{O}_2$)?
questions.solution: As the solubility of $\text{CO}_2$ is 20-25 times higher than that of $\text{O}_2$, the amount of $\text{CO}_2$ that can diffuse through the diffusion membrane per unit difference in partial pressure is much higher compared to $\text{O}_2$.

questions.question:
Read the following statements regarding the transport of gases in human blood:
Statement I: About $97\%$ of $\text{O}_2$ is transported by RBCs in the blood and the remaining $3\%$ is carried in a dissolved state through the plasma.
Statement II: Nearly $70\%$ of $\text{CO}_2$ is transported as bicarbonate ($\text{HCO}_3^-$), $20-25\%$ by RBCs as carbamino-haemoglobin, and $7\%$ in dissolved state through plasma.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.solution: Both statements are correct based on NCERT. $\text{O}_2$ is transported: $97\%$ as oxyhaemoglobin and $3\%$ dissolved in plasma. $\text{CO}_2$ is transported: $70\%$ as bicarbonate ions, $20-25\%$ bound to haemoglobin as carbamino-haemoglobin, and $7\%$ dissolved in plasma.

questions.question: A single molecule of haemoglobin ($	ext{Hb}$) can bind reversibly with a maximum of how many molecules of oxygen ($	ext{O}_2$)?
questions.solution: Haemoglobin is a red-coloured iron-containing pigment. Each haemoglobin molecule contains 4 heme subunits and can bind reversibly with a maximum of 4 molecules of $\text{O}_2$ to form oxyhaemoglobin.

questions.question: Which of the following sets of physiological conditions at the tissue level promotes the DISSOCIATION of oxyhaemoglobin (shifting the oxygen-haemoglobin curve to the right)?
options: Low $p\text{O}_2$, high $p\text{CO}_2$, high $[\text{H}^+]$ (low pH), and higher temperature
High $p\text{O}_2$, low $p\text{CO}_2$, low $[\text{H}^+]$, and lower temperature
questions.solution: In tissues, low $p\text{O}_2$, high $p\text{CO}_2$, high $[	ext{H}^+]$ (acidic pH / Bohr effect), and elevated temperature favor the dissociation of oxygen from oxyhaemoglobin.

questions.question: Every $100\text{ mL}$ of oxygenated blood can deliver around how much volume of oxygen ($	ext{O}_2$) to the tissues under normal resting physiological conditions?
questions.solution: Under normal physiological conditions, every $100\text{ mL}$ of oxygenated blood delivers approximately $5\text{ mL}$ of $\text{O}_2$ to the tissues, out of its total $\sim 20\text{ mL}$ oxygen-carrying capacity.

questions.question: Every $100\text{ mL}$ of deoxygenated blood delivers approximately how much volume of carbon dioxide ($	ext{CO}_2$) to the alveoli?
questions.solution: Every $100\text{ mL}$ of deoxygenated venous blood delivers approximately $4\text{ mL}$ of $\text{CO}_2$ to the alveoli for expiration.

questions.question: Which zinc-containing enzyme present in very high concentration inside RBCs and in minute quantities in plasma facilitates the reversible conversion of $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ into bicarbonate ions ($\text{HCO}_3^-$)?
questions.solution: RBCs contain a very high concentration of the enzyme carbonic anhydrase (and minute quantities in plasma), which facilitates: $$\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightleftharpoons{\text{Carbonic anhydrase}} \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3 \xrightleftharpoons{\text{Carbonic anhydrase}} \text{HCO}_3^- + \text{H}^+$$

questions.question: The primary respiratory rhythm centre responsible for the baseline regulation of respiration is located in which part of the human brain?
questions.solution: A specialized center present in the medulla region of the brain, called the respiratory rhythm centre, is primarily responsible for the basic rhythm and regulation of breathing.

questions.question: The pneumotaxic centre located in the pons region of the brainstem functions to:
options: Moderate the functions of the respiratory rhythm centre by reducing the duration of inspiration
Detect changes in arterial oxygen partial pressure only
Regulate speech and vocal cord tension exclusively
questions.solution: The pneumotaxic centre present in the pons region can moderate the functions of the respiratory rhythm centre. Neural signals from this centre reduce the duration of inspiration and thereby alter the respiratory rate.

questions.question: The chemosensitive area adjacent to the rhythm centre in the medulla is highly sensitive to changes in the concentration of:
questions.solution: A chemosensitive area is situated adjacent to the rhythm centre which is highly sensitive to $\text{CO}_2$ and hydrogen ions ($[\text{H}^+]$). An increase in these substances activates this centre to signal the rhythm centre to adjust breathing and eliminate them. The role of oxygen in regulating respiratory rhythm is quite insignificant.

questions.question: Receptors associated with the aortic arch and carotid artery can recognize changes in ________ and send necessary signals to the rhythm centre for remedial actions:
questions.solution: Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid bodies (on carotid arteries) and aortic bodies (on aortic arch) detect arterial $\text{CO}_2$ and $[\text{H}^+]$ concentrations and transmit impulses to the respiratory rhythm centre.

questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the respiratory disorders and their clinical/pathological features:

List-I (Disorder)List-II (Defining Feature / Pathology)
(A) Asthma(I) Chronic disorder in which alveolar walls are damaged leading to decreased respiratory surface area
(B) Emphysema(II) Difficulty in breathing causing wheezing due to inflammation of bronchi and bronchioles
(C) Occupational Respiratory Disorder(III) Long exposure to dust leading to proliferation of fibrous tissue (fibrosis) in upper lung zones

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution: Asthma: Wheezing and breathlessness due to allergic inflammation of bronchi and bronchioles; Emphysema: Chronic lung disease where alveolar walls are damaged and lose elasticity, majorly caused by cigarette smoking; Occupational respiratory disorders: Silicosis/asbestosis causing severe lung fibrosis.

questions.question: A major and leading causative factor for the development of chronic emphysema in humans is:
questions.solution: Emphysema is a chronic respiratory disease in which alveolar septa are destroyed, reducing the effective surface area for gas exchange. One of its major causes is cigarette smoking.

questions.question: Workers in stone-breaking, grinding, and sand-blasting industries frequently suffer from silicosis and asbestosis, which lead to:
options: Proliferation of fibrous connective tissue (fibrosis) in the lungs causing serious lung damage
Acute bacterial destruction of alveoli only
Excessive accumulation of fluid in the pericardium
questions.solution: In grinding or stone-breaking industries, long-term inhalation of silica or asbestos dust produces chronic inflammation resulting in fibrosis (proliferation of fibrous connective tissue), leading to serious irreversible lung damage.

questions.question: The oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve is characteristically shaped as a:
questions.solution: When percentage saturation of haemoglobin with $\text{O}_2$ is plotted against the partial pressure of oxygen ($p\text{O}_2$), a characteristic sigmoid (S-shaped) curve is obtained due to cooperative binding of oxygen to the 4 heme groups.

questions.question: Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) of human lungs is calculated as:
questions.solution: Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) is the volume of air that remains in the lungs after a normal, quiet expiration: $$\text{FRC} = \text{ERV} + \text{RV} \approx 2100 - 2300\text{ mL}$$

questions.question: Inspiratory Capacity (IC) includes which of the following component volumes?
questions.solution: Inspiratory Capacity (IC) is the total volume of air a person can inspire after a normal expiration: $$\text{IC} = \text{TV} + \text{IRV} \approx 3000 - 3500\text{ mL}$$

questions.question: Total Lung Capacity (TLC) is the total volume of air accommodated in the lungs at the end of a forced inspiration and equals:
questions.solution: Total Lung Capacity (TLC) is the total volume of air accommodated in the lungs at the end of a maximum inhalation: $$\text{TLC} = \text{RV} + \text{ERV} + \text{TV} + \text{IRV} = \text{VC} + \text{RV} \approx 5000 - 6000\text{ mL}$$

questions.question: The thoracic chamber is an anatomically airtight chamber bounded dorsally by the ________, ventrally by the ________, laterally by the ________, and on the lower side by the dome-shaped ________:
questions.solution: The thoracic chamber is anatomically configured as an airtight cage bounded: Dorsally by the vertebral column, Ventrally by the sternum, Laterally by the ribs, and on the lower side by the dome-shaped diaphragm.

questions.question: The anatomical arrangement of human lungs within the airtight thoracic cage is biologically essential because:
options: Any change in the volume of the thoracic cavity will be directly reflected in the lung (pulmonary) cavity, as we cannot directly alter pulmonary volume
It isolates lungs from systemic blood pressure
It prevents air from reaching the stomach during swallowing
It keeps the alveoli filled with water at all times
questions.solution: Human lungs lack independent contractile muscle walls. The airtight anatomical setup ensures that any change in the volume of the thoracic cavity is translated into a corresponding change in pulmonary volume, which is essential for breathing.

questions.question: In humans, the trachea is a straight tube extending down to the mid-thoracic cavity, which divides at the level of the ________ thoracic vertebra into right and left primary bronchi:
questions.solution: The human trachea is supported by incomplete cartilaginous rings and divides at the level of the 5th thoracic vertebra (T5) into right and left primary bronchi.

questions.question: Trachea, primary, secondary, and tertiary bronchi, and initial bronchioles are supported by:
questions.solution: The trachea, primary, secondary, and tertiary bronchi, and initial bronchioles are supported by incomplete C-shaped hyaline cartilaginous rings to prevent collapse during negative intrapleural pressure.

questions.question: The double-layered pleural membrane encloses the human lungs and contains pleural fluid between the outer parietal and inner visceral pleura. The primary function of pleural fluid is to:
options: Reduce friction on the lung surface during respiratory movements
Supply oxygen directly to alveolar capillaries
Filter blood coming from the pulmonary artery
questions.solution: The pleural fluid in the pleural cavity reduces friction on the lung surface as the lungs expand and contract against the inner thoracic wall during respiration.

questions.question: The respiratory conduction zone (from external nostrils up to the terminal bronchioles) performs all of the following functions EXCEPT:
options: Actual site of diffusion of $\text{O}_2$ and $\text{CO}_2$ between blood and atmospheric air
Clearing inhaled atmospheric air from foreign particles and dust
Bringing the temperature of inhaled air to body temperature
questions.solution: The conducting zone transports air to alveoli, clears it of dust, humidifies it, and warms it to body temperature. The actual diffusion of $\text{O}_2$ and $\text{CO}_2$ occurs exclusively in the respiratory/exchange zone (alveoli and their ducts).

questions.question: During forceful expiration in humans (e.g., during exercise or blowing air), which muscles contract actively?
options: Internal intercostal muscles and abdominal muscles
questions.solution: Normal resting expiration is a passive process resulting from the elastic recoil of lungs. Forceful expiration is an active process requiring contraction of internal intercostal muscles (pulling ribs down and in) and abdominal muscles (pushing viscera and diaphragm up).

questions.question: A healthy human breathes on average how many times per minute at rest?
questions.solution: A healthy human breathes approximately 12 to 16 times per minute under resting conditions.

questions.question: How much volume of air can a healthy human inspire or expire per MINUTE during normal quiet breathing?
questions.solution: Tidal volume is $500\text{ mL}$ per breath. Breathing rate is $12-16\text{ breaths/min}$. Therefore, minute respiratory volume $= 500 \times (12 \text{ to } 16) = 6000 - 8000\text{ mL of air per minute}$.

questions.question:
Read the following statements:
Statement I: Binding of oxygen with haemoglobin is primarily related to partial pressure of $\text{O}_2$ ($p\text{O}_2$).
Statement II: High $p\text{CO}_2$, high $[\text{H}^+]$, and higher temperature in alveoli promote the formation of oxyhaemoglobin.

Choose the correct option:
options: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.solution: Statement I is correct. Statement II is incorrect because in the alveoli, HIGH $p\text{O}_2$, LOW $p\text{CO}_2$, LOW $[\text{H}^+]$ (high pH), and LOWER temperature promote oxyhaemoglobin formation.

questions.question: The amount of carbon dioxide transported in the form of carbamino-haemoglobin by RBCs is primarily dependent on:
options: $p\text{CO}_2$ and $p\text{O}_2$ (higher $p\text{CO}_2$ and lower $p\text{O}_2$ favors binding in tissues)
questions.solution: $\text{CO}_2$ binds directly to the amino group of haemoglobin to form carbamino-haemoglobin. When $p\text{CO}_2$ is high and $p\text{O}_2$ is low in tissues, more $\text{CO}_2$ binding occurs. In alveoli where $p\text{O}_2$ is high and $p\text{CO}_2$ is low, dissociation of $\text{CO}_2$ takes place.

questions.question: At the tissue level where $p\text{CO}_2$ is high, carbon dioxide diffuses into erythrocytes and reacts with water to form $\text{HCO}_3^-$ and $\text{H}^+$. At the alveolar surface, the reaction proceeds in the reverse direction because:
options: $p\text{CO}_2$ is low in alveoli, causing conversion of $\text{HCO}_3^-$ and $\text{H}^+$ back into $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$
Carbonic anhydrase is absent in the pulmonary capillaries
High acidity in alveoli blocks enzyme activity
questions.solution: At the alveolar site where $p\text{CO}_2$ is low, the equilibrium of the reaction catalyzed by carbonic anhydrase shifts in the reverse direction, leading to the formation of $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, releasing $\text{CO}_2$ into the alveolar air.

questions.question: Expiratory Capacity (EC) is mathematically represented as:
questions.solution: Expiratory Capacity (EC) is the total volume of air a person can expire after a normal quiet inhalation: $$\text{EC} = \text{TV} + \text{ERV} \approx 1500 - 1600\text{ mL}$$

questions.question: The volume of air inspired or expired during a normal resting respiration in a human is called:
questions.solution: Tidal Volume (TV) is defined as the volume of air inspired or expired during a normal quiet breath, averaging approximately $500\text{ mL}$ in healthy adult humans.

questions.question: Which of the following cartilages of the human larynx is a thin, leaf-like elastic cartilaginous flap that prevents the entry of food into the glottis during swallowing?
questions.solution: The epiglottis is a thin elastic cartilaginous flap that covers the glottis (the opening of the windpipe) during swallowing, preventing food or liquid from entering the larynx and trachea.

questions.question: Inspiration can occur only when intra-pulmonary pressure is:
options: Negative relative to atmospheric pressure (less than atmospheric pressure)
questions.solution: Inspiration occurs when there is a negative pressure in the lungs with respect to atmospheric pressure, i.e., when intra-pulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric pressure, drawing air into the lungs.

questions.question: Expiration takes place when:
options: Intra-pulmonary pressure is higher than atmospheric pressure
Intra-pulmonary pressure is lower than atmospheric pressure
questions.solution: Expiration occurs when relaxation of the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles reduces thoracic volume, increasing intra-pulmonary pressure slightly above atmospheric pressure, which drives air out of the lungs.

questions.question: What is the value of partial pressure of oxygen ($p\text{O}_2$) and carbon dioxide ($p\text{CO}_2$) in normal atmospheric air at sea level?
questions.solution: In dry atmospheric air at sea level: $p\text{O}_2 = 159\text{ mm Hg}$ (approx. $21\%$) and $p\text{CO}_2 = 0.3\text{ mm Hg}$ (approx. $0.04\%$).

questions.question: The dead space volume (anatomical dead space air that remains in the respiratory conducting tract and does not participate in gas exchange) in a healthy human averages approximately:
questions.solution: Out of the $500\text{ mL}$ Tidal Volume, about $150\text{ mL}$ remains in the non-exchange conducting airways (trachea, bronchi, bronchioles) and is called the anatomical dead space volume. Only $\sim 350\text{ mL}$ reaches the alveolar exchange surfaces.

questions.question: Which of the following changes will shift the Oxygen-Haemoglobin Dissociation Curve to the LEFT (increasing haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen)?
options: High $p\text{O}_2$, low $p\text{CO}_2$, low $[\text{H}^+]$ (alkaline pH), and lower temperature
High $p\text{CO}_2$, high $[\text{H}^+]$ (acidic pH), and higher temperature
Heavy physical exercise and lactic acidosis
questions.solution: A left shift of the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve signifies increased binding affinity of haemoglobin for $\text{O}_2$, which occurs under conditions characteristic of alveolar blood: high $p\text{O}_2$, low $p\text{CO}_2$, low $[\text{H}^+]$ (high pH), and lower temperature.
